chapters.title: Chapter 4: Alternative and Real Assets Through the Cycle

lessons.title: Commodities and Currencies: INR, Crude, and the Import Bill

body.text: India doesn't just react to global commodity cycles, it imports them directly into its currency. Understand the oil-to-rupee feedback loop, and a Middle East crisis or a China demand surge starts to explain moves in your portfolio through a channel none of the earlier chapters covered directly.

children.text: Chapter 1 introduced the commodity and monetary policy channels linking India to the global cycle, and the last lesson covered gold, the one commodity most Indian investors actually hold. This final lesson of the chapter covers the rest: how crude oil prices move through India's trade balance into the rupee itself, and what that means for your portfolio even if you never touch a commodity directly.

markDefs.definition: The difference between a country's total foreign currency earnings (exports, services, remittances) and its total foreign currency payments (imports); a wider deficit means more foreign currency is leaving than entering.

children.text: India imports roughly 85% of the crude oil it consumes. That single structural fact drives a chain reaction that shows up in this lesson's title: rising crude prices widen India's trade deficit and its

, both because more dollars leave the country and because import bills rise. A wider deficit means more demand for dollars to pay for those imports, which pressures the rupee to weaken, which in turn can push the RBI to sell foreign exchange reserves or raise interest rates to slow the fall.

body.caption: The chain reaction, step by step

cells: India's import bill rises, since it imports most of its crude
The trade deficit and current account deficit widen
Demand for dollars to pay for imports rises, pressuring the rupee to weaken
The RBI may sell forex reserves and/or raise rates to slow the rupee's fall

children.text: You've met pieces of 2022 in three earlier lessons: Brent crude above $120 a barrel, gold's low-double-digit INR gain, and the RBI's rate hikes from 4.00% to 6.50%. This lesson supplies the missing link that ties them together. The crude spike widened India's current account deficit to around 2% of GDP in FY23, from about 1.2% the year before, and the rupee fell from roughly ₹74 to ₹82.7 per dollar over the year. To slow that fall, the RBI drew down its foreign exchange reserves substantially, from a peak of around $642 billion in September 2021 to around $525 billion by October 2022, a decline of more than $100 billion, alongside the rate hikes already covered in Chapter 3.

stats.context: A decline of over $100 billion, partly from defending the rupee

stats.label: Current account deficit, FY23

body.text: Notice that a single global event, one commodity price spike, has now shown up across four different lessons in this course: as an overheat-to-stagflation quadrant call in Chapter 1, as a rate-hiking case study in Chapter 3, as a gold tailwind in the last lesson, and now as a currency and reserves story. That's not repetition for its own sake, it's the same real event moving through every asset class this course covers, which is exactly the point of thinking in cycles rather than in asset-class silos.

children.text: Winners and Losers Within the Same Currency Move

body.title: A weaker rupee doesn't hit every sector the same way

columns.label: Helped by a weaker rupee
points: IT services: dollar revenues translate into more rupees
Pharma exporters: similarly earn a large share of revenue in dollars
Other export-oriented manufacturers with mostly rupee costs

columns.label: Hurt by a weaker rupee
points: Oil marketing companies: crude is priced and paid for in dollars
Airlines: jet fuel is a large share of costs and is dollar-linked
Any business with significant unhedged dollar-denominated debt

body.title: Crude Spikes Again
body.scenario: A fresh geopolitical shock pushes Brent crude above $110 a barrel and keeps it there for several months. The rupee weakens meaningfully as a result.
body.prompt: Name one sector that would likely benefit from this combination and one that would likely be hurt, and explain the mechanism for each using what you've learned in this lesson.
body.modelAnswer: IT services would likely benefit: their revenue is largely dollar-denominated, so a weaker rupee directly boosts rupee-reported earnings even if their underlying dollar business hasn't changed at all, a partial natural hedge against exactly this kind of currency move. Airlines would likely be hurt on two fronts at once: jet fuel, already a large share of their operating costs, becomes more expensive in dollar terms as crude rises, and the weaker rupee makes that same dollar-priced fuel bill even larger in rupee terms, a double hit that oil marketing companies and other big dollar-cost importers share.

children.text: Getting Some Currency Diversification Into a Portfolio

markDefs.definition: The RBI scheme allowing resident Indians to remit up to $250,000 per financial year abroad for permitted purposes, including investing in foreign stocks, mutual funds, or property.

children.text: Most of this course has looked at rupee-denominated assets. India's

lets resident individuals invest up to $250,000 a year abroad, and Indian mutual funds also offer feeder funds that invest in US and other foreign equities without needing to open a foreign brokerage account. Holding some dollar-denominated assets this way gives an Indian portfolio a genuine natural hedge: if the rupee weakens for any of the reasons covered in this lesson, the rupee value of dollar-denominated holdings rises to at least partly offset it, independent of how those foreign assets perform in their own currency.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: An investor wants a holding that tends to rise in rupee terms specifically when the rupee weakens against the dollar, independent of that holding's own performance in its home currency. Which of the following best fits?
options: A dollar-denominated foreign equity fund held via the LRS route
body.explanation: A dollar-denominated foreign holding gets an automatic rupee value boost whenever the rupee weakens against the dollar, on top of whatever that asset does in its own currency. The other three options are rupee-denominated and carry no such currency offset.

body.text: The oil-to-rupee chain isn't perfectly mechanical or instant. Petrol and diesel prices at the pump don't always track crude in real time, since public sector oil marketing companies sometimes absorb price spikes for a period, particularly around elections or periods of political sensitivity, before eventually passing costs through. Treat the feedback loop as a strong underlying tendency, not a formula that recalculates the rupee the moment crude ticks up.

cards.definition: The gap between a country's foreign currency earnings and payments; a wider CAD typically pressures the domestic currency to weaken.
Foreign currency and gold assets held by the RBI, used partly to intervene in currency markets and defend the rupee when needed.
A company that refines and distributes petroleum products in India; several are public sector and sometimes absorb crude price spikes before passing them on to consumers.
Liberalised Remittance Scheme, allowing resident Indians to remit up to $250,000 a year abroad, including for investing in foreign assets.
An asset or business characteristic that automatically offsets a specific risk without requiring a separate hedging transaction, such as dollar revenue offsetting rupee depreciation.

points: India imports roughly 85% of the crude oil it consumes, so rising global crude prices widen India's trade and current account deficits and pressure the rupee to weaken

In 2022, this chain played out in full: Brent above $120 widened the CAD to about 2% of GDP, the rupee fell from about ₹74 to ₹82.7 per dollar, and the RBI's forex reserves fell by more than $100 billion from their September 2021 peak while defending the currency

A single event, like the 2022 crude spike, moves through every asset class this course covers, showing up as a growth-inflation quadrant call, a rate-hiking case study, a gold tailwind, and a currency and reserves story all at once
A weaker rupee helps dollar-revenue exporters like IT and pharma, and hurts dollar-cost importers like oil marketing companies and airlines, sometimes through more than one channel at once
The LRS route and foreign feeder funds let Indian investors hold dollar-denominated assets, which act as a natural hedge, rising in rupee terms specifically when the rupee weakens
The oil-to-rupee chain is a strong tendency, not an instant formula, since administered fuel pricing can delay how quickly crude moves actually reach the pump and the wider economy
